title: Asia's AI Bubble Just Popped. India Barely Flinched.
excerpt: South Korea's KOSPI crashed 8% and foreign investors dumped $137 billion from Asian stocks in six months. India rose. Here's why the rotation may be just beginning.
body:
When South Korea's KOSPI index nosedived nearly 8% on Thursday — its worst single-day drop since the pandemic panic of 2020 — traders across Asia scrambled for cover. Taiwan's benchmark fell hard. The MSCI Asia-Pacific index slumped 2.4%.

India's Sensex climbed 0.75%.

The divergence was not a fluke. It was the sharpest expression yet of a rotation that has been building quietly for weeks: out of the AI-heavy markets that defined the first half of 2026, and into economies that offer something the chip rally cannot — stability, diversification, and a macro tailwind that is only getting stronger.

## The trigger

The immediate catalyst was Meta's announcement late Wednesday that it would shift a significant portion of its AI infrastructure spending away from external chip procurement and toward internally designed silicon — a move that sent Nvidia, Samsung, and SK Hynix tumbling in after-hours trading and triggered a cascade across Asia's semiconductor belt on Thursday morning.

South Korea bore the brunt. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together account for roughly 55% of the KOSPI's market capitalisation, fell sharply. The two chipmakers have been the primary beneficiaries of a blistering AI-driven rally that nearly doubled South Korea's benchmark in the first half of the year.

But that concentration — the very feature that powered the gains — became the vulnerability. Foreign investors had already been heading for the exits. According to LSEG data, overseas funds pulled a net $137.36 billion from Asian equities in the first six months of 2026, the fastest pace of outflows in at least 16 years. South Korea alone shed $70.8 billion, and Taiwan lost $29.6 billion.

## Why India held up

India's resilience on Thursday was not accidental. It was the product of three converging forces.

First, oil. Brent crude dropped below $71 per barrel after Qatar confirmed that Iran and the United States had made "positive progress" in indirect talks in Doha. For India, which imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, every dollar off the oil price feeds directly into a lower current-account deficit, lower inflation, and higher corporate margins. Goldman Sachs raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points this week, citing the oil windfall and improving external balances.

Second, valuation. After months of being sold as "overvalued" relative to the AI-powered markets, India is now the cheaper trade. Average emerging-market fund allocations to India dropped below 10% in April — their lowest since early 2021, down from a peak of 17.5% in 2024, according to Copley Fund Research. That gap is now an opportunity.

"India is among the most oversold markets we track," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management. "This macro improvement, alongside a more attractive valuation premium, strengthens the case to act."

Third, the IT rebound. India's Nifty IT index surged 4.6% on Thursday — its best day in months — as investors rotated into software services stocks that had been hammered earlier this year on fears of AI disruption. The same AI narrative that crushed Indian IT in the first quarter is now, paradoxically, pulling money back in: if Meta is building its own chips, external chipmakers lose, but Indian outsourcing firms that help build and deploy AI applications could gain.

## The bigger picture

The numbers tell a striking story. In a half-year when $137 billion left Asian equities, India's market clawed its way back to a $5 trillion market capitalisation. The rupee posted its first quarterly gain in five quarters. Foreign investors poured a record $3 billion into Indian government bonds in June alone, attracted by tax breaks and the prospect of Bloomberg index inclusion.

"Tech volatility has prompted a search for alternatives, with India ending June with roughly 3% outperformance and up 7% from the lows in early June," global brokerage firm Macquarie said in a note.

G. Chokkalingam, founder of Equinomics Research, put it simply: "The drop in oil prices is the single biggest factor for India. It impacts growth, inflation, forex reserves, fiscal deficit — everything."

## What NRIs should watch

For Indian-origin investors holding positions in South Korean or Taiwanese tech through global ETFs — a common allocation in US-based 401(k) plans and brokerage accounts — the rotation is a direct portfolio question. India-focused ETFs listed in the US saw positive inflows last week for the first time in over a month, according to Elara Capital.

The risk, of course, is that the AI selloff proves temporary — a breather in a structural bull market. If Nvidia's next earnings surprise to the upside, the chip rally could resume and India's relative advantage could fade.

But for now, in a world where the three stocks that powered Asia's best-performing markets just became its biggest liabilities, India's old-economy breadth and commodity sensitivity look less like weaknesses and more like exactly what a diversified portfolio needs.
